etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English opposen, from Old French opposer, from Latin ob (“before, against”) + Medieval Latin pono (“to put”), taking the place of Latin opponere (“to oppose”).

definitions.definition: To attempt to stop the progression of; to resist or antagonize by physical means, or by arguments, etc.; to contend against.

quote.citation: 1613 (date written), William Shakespeare, [John Fletcher], “The Famous History of the Life of King Henry the Eight”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene iv]:
quote.text: I am  […]  too weak / To oppose your cunning.

definitions.definition: To present or set up in opposition; to pose.

quote.text: I may  […]  oppose my single opinion to his.

quote.citation: 1839, Philip Meadows Taylor, Confessions of a Thug:
quote.text: [T]hree walls had been left standing, with large intervals between each; and they would certainly oppose a most formidable interruption to an invader.

definitions.definition: To place in front of, or over against; to set opposite; to exhibit.

quote.citation: 1613 (date written), William Shakespeare, [John Fletcher], “The Famous History of the Life of King Henry the Eight”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene i]:
quote.text: Her grace sat down  […]  / In a rich chair of state; opposing freely / The beauty of her person to the people.
